## Introduction

The Antarctic Continent is the fifth larger continent in extension, with about 13.7 millions of km2. It is a continent of extremes, since it is the higher, colder, drier, strong winds and remote continent (Machado and Brito, [2006](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR10 "Machado MCS, Brito T (2006) Antártica: Ensino Fundamental e Ensino Médio. In the continental Antarctica (2% of the total area of Antarctica), there are observed several specific relationships to exposure of soil types, geomorphology, and water supply, so there is a positive relationship between the Antarctic flora and bird colonies (Pereira et al., [1990](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR16 "Pereira AB, Putzke J, Sander M (1990) Plants utilized by Larus dominicanus Lichtenstein (1823) for nest building at the South Shetland Island, Antarctica. 15|## Abstract
16|
17|### Background
18|
19|This paper presents a comparative study of moss diversity in three collection sites in the South Shetland Islands (King George, Elephant, and Nelson Islands) and one in the Antarctic Continent (Hope Bay, Antarctic Peninsula). In the King George, Elephant, and Nelson Islands, the collections were done in ice-free areas during the austral summers of years 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1992, and 1994. In Hope Bay, the collections were done in the 2009 summer (February). All collections were deposited in the HCB (Chaves Batista Herbarium).
20|
21|### Findings
22|
23|The King George Area is the most diverse area and the Hope Bay has the lowest diversity stats. The diversity stats for each region and the similarities between both are presented.
24|
25|### Conclusion
26|
27|This results suggested that harder climatic conditions determine lower diversity for the bryoflora.
28|
29|## Resumen
30|
31|En este trabajo se presenta un estudio comparativo de tres puntos de muestreo de musgos
32|
33|en las Islas Shetland del Sur (Isla Rey Jorge, Elefante y Nelson) y el Continente Antártico (Bahía Esperanza, Península Antártica). En las Islas King George, Elefante y Nelson, se tomaron muestras en las zonas libres de hielo durante los veranos australes de años 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1992 y 1994. Hope Bay, las colecciones se hicieron en el verano austral de 2009 (febrero). Todas las colecciones fueron depositadas en el herbario de HCB (Herbario Chaves Batista). Los índices de diversidad para cada región se presentan, así como la similitud entre ellos.

51|## Introduction
52|
53|The Antarctic Continent is the fifth larger continent in extension, with about 13.7 millions of km2. It is a continent of extremes, since it is the higher, colder, drier, strong winds and remote continent (Machado and Brito, [2006](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR10 "Machado MCS, Brito T (2006) Antártica: Ensino Fundamental e Ensino Médio. Ministério da Educação, Secretaria da Educação Básica, Brasília")). In addition to these extreme climatic conditions, the UV-A and UV-B radiations are potential aspects affecting the structure and development of plants (Green et al., [2005](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR5 "Green TGA, Kulle D, Pannewitz S, Sancho LG, Schroeter B (2005) UV-A protection in mosses growing in continental Antarctica. Polar Biol 28(11):822–827")).
54|
55|Studies of plant communities in Antarctica have a very relatively short history, if compared to other parts of the world particularly tropical and temperate regions. However, there are areas of the Maritime Antarctic region with excellent descriptions of the vegetation, such as the South Shetlands Island (Lindsay [1971](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR8 "Lindsay DC (1971) Vegetation of the South Shetland Islands. British Antartic Survey, v. n25, pp 59–83"), Furmanczyk and Ochyra [1982](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR2 "Furmanczyk K, Ochyra R (1982) Plant communities of the Admiralty Bay region (King George Island, South Shetland Island, Antarctic). I Jasnorzewski Gardens. Polish Polar Research 3:25–39"), Hu [1998](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR6 "Hu SS (1998) Moss communities types and species diversity of Southern Fields Peninsula (King George Island, South Shetland Islands) Antarctica. Journal of Hattori Botany Laboratory, v. 84, pp 187-198")), Signy Islands (Lewis-Smith, [1972](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR7 "Lewis-Smith RI (1972) Vegetation of the South Orkney Island with particular references to Signy Island. British Antarctic Survey Bulletin, v. 33/34, pp 89-122")), Nelson Island (Putzke et al.*,*
56|[1995](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR20 "Putzke J, Putzke MTL, Pereira AB (1995) Moss communities of Rip Point in Northern Nelson Island, South Shetland Islands, Antarctica. Polar Biology, v. 2, pp 20-40")), and Elephant Island (Allison and Lewis-Smith, [1973](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR1 "Allison JS, Lewis-Smith RI (1973) The vegetation of Elephant Island, South Shetland Islands. British Antarctic Survey Bulletin, v. 33-34, pp 185–212"), Pereira and Putzke, [1994](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR15 "Pereira AB, Putzke J (1994) Floristic composition of Stinker Point, Elephant Island, Antarctica. Korean J Polar Res 5(2):37–47"))
57|
58|The Antarctic flora is composed mainly of bryophytes and lichen species adapted to short summers and low temperatures (Putzke and Pereira [2001](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR18 "Putzke J, Pereira AB (2001) The Antarctic mosses with special reference to the South Shetland Islands. (ed) Ulbra, Canoas")). Such climatic conditions inhibit the reproductive cycle, limiting the diversity and the gene pool, especially for flowering plants (Pereira and Putzke [1994](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR15 "Pereira AB, Putzke J (1994) Floristic composition of Stinker Point, Elephant Island, Antarctica. Korean J Polar Res 5(2):37–47")). The Antarctic hair grass (*Deschampsia antarctica* Desv.) and the Antarctic pearlwort (*Colobanthus quitensis* [Kunth.] Bartl.) are the only native angiosperms growing in Antarctica but are restricted to the maritime Antarctica, which experience a shorter daylight period, warmer temperatures, and higher water availability in comparison to continental Antarctica.
59|
60|In the continental Antarctica (2% of the total area of Antarctica), there are observed several specific relationships to exposure of soil types, geomorphology, and water supply, so there is a positive relationship between the Antarctic flora and bird colonies (Pereira et al., [1990](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR16 "Pereira AB, Putzke J, Sander M (1990) Plants utilized by Larus dominicanus Lichtenstein (1823) for nest building at the South Shetland Island, Antarctica. Pesqui Antártica Bras 2(1):79–85")), where the nutrients are achieved directly from animal resources (Galimberti, [1991](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR3 "Galimberti D (1991) Antarctica an introductory guide. Zagier & Urruty Publications, Florida")). Only a few plants can survive in Antarctica, and they provide a geographic distribution directly related to abiotic factors. Due to its ability to grow in such extreme environments, mosses are among the most important plants which occur in ice-free areas of Antarctica (Putzke and Pereira, [2001](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR18 "Putzke J, Pereira AB (2001) The Antarctic mosses with special reference to the South Shetland Islands. (ed) Ulbra, Canoas")), although moss communities are generally considered of low complexity and species diversity (Smith, [1984](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR23 "Smith RIL (1984) Terrestrial plant biology. In: Laws RM (ed) Antarctic ecology, vol 1. Academic Press, London")).
61|
62|In Antarctica, the mosses are associated to melting areas, such that they depend of water supply during the austral summer to realize photosynthesis and growing (Schaefer et al., [2004](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR22 "Schaefer CEGR, Simas FBN, Albuquerque-Filho MR, Michel RFM, Viana J, Tatur HM (2004) Fosfatização: processo de formação de solos na Baía do Almirantado e implicações ambientais. In: Schaefer CN, Francelino MR, Simas FNB, Albuquerque F, De MR (ed) Ecossistemas Costeiros e Monitoramento Ambiental da Antártica Marítima: Baía do Almirantado, IIha Rei George. NEPUT-Departamento de Solos, Viçosa, pp 47–58"); Meick and Seppelt, [1997](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR11 "Meick DR, Seppelt RD (1997) Vegetation patterns in relation to climatic and endogenous changes in Wilkes Land, Continental Antarctica. J Ecol 85:43–56")). Given the difficulties imposed by the environment, the mosses from Antarctica present pigments that are involved in UV radiation protection (Glime, [2007](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR4 "Glime JM (2007) Bryophyte ecology. Volume 1. Physiological ecology. Ebook sponsored by Michigan Technological University and the International Association of Bryologists. Accessed on 12-12-2013 at 
63|                  http://www.bryoecol.mtu.edu/
64|                  
65|                
66|                "); Lovelock and Robinson, [2002](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR9 "Lovelock CE, Robinson SA (2002) Surface reflectance properties of Antarctic moss and their relationship to plant species, pigment composition and photosynthetic function. Plant Cell Environ 25:1239–1250")), while some species are adapted to support dehydration at different levels (Robinson et al., [2000](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR21 "Robinson S, Wasley J, Popp M, Lovelock CE (2000) Desiccation tolerance of three moss species from continental Antarctica. Aust J Plant Physiol 27:379–388")).
67|
68|The moss Antarctic flora can be divided into six distinct phytogeographical elements (Ochyra, [1998](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR12 "Ochyra R (1998) The moss flora of King George Island Antarctica. Academy of Sciences, Cracow")) comprising a number of species for each element, as follows: Antarctic endemic distribution (11 species); Subantarctic distribution (18 species); south-temperate distribution (26 species); bipolar distribution; cosmopolitan distribution (5 species); tropical distribution (1 species). From this division, it can be observed that most of the mosses found in Antarctica have bipolar distribution, being a striking feature of the Antarctic moss flora (Ochyra et al., [2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR13 "Ochyra R, Lewis Smith RI, Bednarek Ochyra H (2008) The illustrated moss flora of Antarctica. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, p 685")). However, the richness and other diversity stats have not yet been widely exploited to understand the distribution of moss species in Antarctic.
69|
70|In this study, the distribution of moss species among four different points from South Shetland and the Antarctic continent was compared through a review of collections, aiming to provide subsidies for the understanding of how species are distributed in the Maritime Antarctic.
71|
72|## Methods
73|
74|The moss diversity of three island in the South Shetland archipelago (King George - 62° 05′ 13, 55″S and 58° 24′ 17, 51″W; Elephant - 61° 11′ 51, 74″S and 55° 17′ 56, 37″W; and Nelson Islands - 62° 14′ 29, 47″S and 58° 59′ 39, 26″W) and one in the Antarctic Peninsula (Hope Bay - 63° 23′ 0″S, 56° 59′ 0″W) were compared.
75|
76|The collections were done in the ice-free areas during the austral summers of years 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1992, and 1994 in the King George, Elephant, and Nelson Islands. In Hope Bay, the collections were made in the 2009 summer (February). The distribution and occurrences reported by Ochyra et al. ([2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR13 "Ochyra R, Lewis Smith RI, Bednarek Ochyra H (2008) The illustrated moss flora of Antarctica. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, p 685")) were also checked for comparison purpose.
77|
78|All collections were deposited in the HCB Herbarium (Chaves Batista Herbarium). The species were indentified according to Putzke and Pereira ([2001](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR18 "Putzke J, Pereira AB (2001) The Antarctic mosses with special reference to the South Shetland Islands. (ed) Ulbra, Canoas")), Ochyra ([1998](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR12 "Ochyra R (1998) The moss flora of King George Island Antarctica. Academy of Sciences, Cracow")), and Ochyra et al. ([2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR13 "Ochyra R, Lewis Smith RI, Bednarek Ochyra H (2008) The illustrated moss flora of Antarctica. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, p 685")). The species names follow Ochyra et al. ([2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR13 "Ochyra R, Lewis Smith RI, Bednarek Ochyra H (2008) The illustrated moss flora of Antarctica. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, p 685")).
79|
80|The data obtained about moss species growing in each sampling area were organized in a presence or absence (1 or 0, respectively) and quantitative matrices (number of individual sampled) and used to describe the occurrence of each species found. These matrices were used to obtain the diversity stats, where we used Shannon-Weaver diversity index (H’) and the Jaccard’s similarity coefficient (J’) with help of the PAST statistic program version 1.91 to evaluate the richness and the similarity of the species.
81|
82|## Findings
83|
84|### Richness data
85|
86|In the taxonomical review, 46 species were identified, belonging to 23 genera and 15 families. These 46 taxa correspond to 41% of the species that were reported to Antarctica (Ochyra, et al., [2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR13 "Ochyra R, Lewis Smith RI, Bednarek Ochyra H (2008) The illustrated moss flora of Antarctica. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, p 685")).
87|
88|From 276 samples reviewed, 315 moss occurrences were observed in the four sampled areas (Figure [1](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#Fig1)). From these, 152 occurred in King George Island, 87 in Elephant Island, 22 in Nelson Island, and 54 in Hope Bay. King George Island also has the greater number of species (42), followed by Elephant (25) and Nelson (18). Hope Bay has the lowest species number of all studied sites (11). The data of species occurrence in each collecting site are listed in Table [1](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#Tab1).
89|
90|![Figure 1](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40693-014-0033-z/MediaObjects/40693_2014_33_Fig1_HTML.gif)
91|
92|**Number of individuals and species in each collecting site.**
93|
94|Out of 15 families found, Bryaceae (10 species in 2 genera) was the most common, followed by Pottiaceae and Grimmiaceae (5 species and 2 genera both). Amblystegiaceae was the family with the higher number of genera observed (4).
95|
96|Many moss species were found associated to other species. In the Hope Bay region, for example, *Ceratodon purpureus* - *Polytrichum strictum* was the most frequently association found. Associations between this genus and *Andreaea depressinervis* - *Andreaea gainii* were also found, as well as between *Andreaea depressinervis* - *Ceratodon purpureus* and *Andreaea depressinervis* - *Sanionia uncinata*.
97|
98|*Andreae acumminata* Cardot. was recognized in Antarctica by Putzke and Pereira ([2001](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR18 "Putzke J, Pereira AB (2001) The Antarctic mosses with special reference to the South Shetland Islands. (ed) Ulbra, Canoas")) for Nelson Island only. Ochyra et al. ([2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR13 "Ochyra R, Lewis Smith RI, Bednarek Ochyra H (2008) The illustrated moss flora of Antarctica. Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, p 685")) exclude this species from moss flora of Antarctica but without reviewing the material under voucher 30292 (HBC); thus, we maintain this species to the moss flora of Antarctica, since the characteristics of the sample analyzed are in accordance to the diagnostic features of this species.
99|
100|### Diversity and similarity stats
101|
102|The Shannon-Weaver index indicated that King George Island is the most diverse area (H’ = 3,178), followed by Elephant Island (H’ = 2,909) and Nelson Island (H’ = 2,839). Hope Bay presented the lowest result (H’ = 1,933) (Figure [2](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#Fig2)).
103|
104|![Figure 2](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40693-014-0033-z/MediaObjects/40693_2014_33_Fig2_HTML.gif)
105|
106|**Shannon diversity index to each collecting point.** Distinct letter means statistical differences found in the sampling.
107|
108|The Shannon-Weaver index, comparing Elephant and Nelson Islands, brought no significant differences in the diversity of both islands (H’ = 2,909 and H’ = 2,839, respectively).
109|
110|Despite this, the number of species is different in each Island (Elephant = 25, Nelson = 18 species), as well the sample number (Elephant = 87, Nelson = 22 individuals), suggesting differences in moss communities in these islands. The other collecting sites presented statistically significant differences.
111|
112|Hope Bay shows the lowest richness, probably because of the harder climate conditions found in the area. In addition, information about species richness can be incomplete because of the difficulty in collecting data in this point. *Sanionia uncinata* has the highest occurrence such that the species was found in all areas studied. *Ceratodon purpureus* was the most common species in Hope Bay.
113|
114|The similarity calculated by the Jaccard coefficient indicates a high similarity between King George and Elephant Island, followed by Nelson Island and Hope Bay (Figure [3](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#Fig3)).
115|
116|![Figure 3](//media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40693-014-0033-z/MediaObjects/40693_2014_33_Fig3_HTML.gif)
117|
118|**Clustering analysis of the Jaccard similarity coefficient to each collecting site.**
119|
120|## Discussion
121|
122|The highest species number and the individual occurrence for each species in King George Island are probably associated to the climatic conditions (warmer, humid, and low wind incidences). It cannot be excluded due to the fact that the location of the Brazilian Base in this island allows a higher collection effort (Pereira and Putzke, [1994](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR15 "Pereira AB, Putzke J (1994) Floristic composition of Stinker Point, Elephant Island, Antarctica. Korean J Polar Res 5(2):37–47"); Pereira et al., [2008](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR17 "Pereira AB, Putzke MTL, Putzke J (2008) Biological communities of Keller Peninsula, King George Island - Antarctica. Caderno Pesquisa Série Biol 20(3):63–74"); Peat et al., [2007](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR14 "Peat HJ, Clarke A, Convey P (2007) Diversity and biogeography of the Antarctic flora. J Biogeogr 34:132–146")).
123|
124|The richness and the Shannon-Weaver index pointed King George Island as the most diverse. Victoria and Pereira ([2007](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR24 "Victoria FC, Pereira AB (2007) Índice de valor ecológico (IES) como ferramenta para estudos fitossociológicos e conservação das espécies de musgos na Baia do Almirantado, Ilha Rei George, Antártica Marítima. Oecologia Brasiliensis 11(1):50–55")) showed that the highest temperatures and weak winds were found in the Admiralty Bay, generating a distinct microclimate in this area, in comparison to the rest of the island, and thus can be reflecting in higher plant diversity in this area. The Elephant and Nelson Island, despite the differences in the individuals sampled, are both often related as islands with a moderate moss diversity, where no specific occurrences were found (Putzke et al, [1998](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR19 "Putzke J, Pereira AB, Putzke MTL (1998) Moss communities of rip point in Northern Island, South Shetland Islands, Antarctica. Pesqui Antártica Bras 3(1):104–115"); Pereira and Putzke [1994](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR15 "Pereira AB, Putzke J (1994) Floristic composition of Stinker Point, Elephant Island, Antarctica. Korean J Polar Res 5(2):37–47")), unlike King George Island that has a known occurrence of endemic species cited in the literature (Ochyra, [1998](/article/10.1186/s40693-014-0033-z#ref-CR12 "Ochyra R (1998) The moss flora of King George Island Antarctica. Academy of Sciences, Cracow")). Abstract
Background: This paper presents a comparative study of moss diversity in three collection sites in the South Shetland
Islands (King George, Elephant, and Nelson Islands) and one in the Antarctic Continent (Hope Bay, Antarctic Peninsula).
In the King George, Elephant, and Nelson Islands, the collections were done in ice-free areas during the austral
summers of years 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1992, and 1994. In Hope Bay, the collections were done in the 2009 summer
(February). All collections were deposited in the HCB (Chaves Batista Herbarium).
Findings: The King George Area is the most diverse area and the Hope Bay has the lowest diversity stats. The diversity
stats for each region and the similarities between both are presented.
Conclusion: This results suggested that harder climatic conditions determine lower diversity for the bryoflora.
Keywords: Bryophyta; Flora; Ice-free area; Shannon-Weaver index
Resumen
En este trabajo se presenta un estudio comparativo de tres puntos de muestreo de musgos
en las Islas Shetland del Sur (Isla Rey Jorge, Elefante y Nelson) y el Continente Antártico (Bahía Esperanza, Península
Antártica). En las Islas King George, Elefante y Nelson, se tomaron muestras en las zonas libres de hielo durante los
veranos australes de años 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991, 1992 y 1994. Hope Bay, las colecciones se hicieron en el verano
austral de 2009 (febrero). Todas las colecciones fueron depositadas en el herbario de HCB (Herbario Chaves Batista).
Los índices de diversidad para cada región se presentan, así como la similitud entre ellos.

Introduction
The Antarctic Continent is the fifth larger continent in
extension, with about 13.7 millions of km2
. It is a continent
of extremes, since it is the higher, colder, drier, strong
winds and remote continent (Machado and Brito, 2006). In
addition to these extreme climatic conditions, the UV-A
and UV-B radiations are potential aspects affecting the
structure and development of plants (Green et al., 2005).
Studies of plant communities in Antarctica have a very
relatively short history, if compared to other parts of the
world particularly tropical and temperate regions. However,
there are areas of the Maritime Antarctic region with
excellent descriptions of the vegetation, such as the South
Shetlands Island (Lindsay 1971, Furmanczyk and Ochyra
1982, Hu 1998), Signy Islands (Lewis-Smith, 1972), Nelson
Island (Putzke et al., 1995), and Elephant Island (Allison
and Lewis-Smith, 1973, Pereira and Putzke, 1994)
The Antarctic flora is composed mainly of bryophytes
and lichen species adapted to short summers and low
temperatures (Putzke and Pereira 2001). Such climatic
conditions inhibit the reproductive cycle, limiting the
diversity and the gene pool, especially for flowering plants
(Pereira and Putzke 1994). The Antarctic hair grass
(Deschampsia antarctica Desv.) and the Antarctic pearl-
wort (Colobanthus quitensis [Kunth.] Bartl.) are the only
native angiosperms growing in Antarctica but are restricted
to the maritime Antarctica, which experience a shorter

In the continental Antarctica (2% of the total area of
Antarctica), there are observed several specific relation-
ships to exposure of soil types, geomorphology, and
water supply, so there is a positive relationship between
the Antarctic flora and bird colonies (Pereira et al., 1990),
where the nutrients are achieved directly from animal
resources (Galimberti, 1991). Only a few plants can
survive in Antarctica, and they provide a geographic
distribution directly related to abiotic factors. Due to its
ability to grow in such extreme environments, mosses are
among the most important plants which occur in ice-free
areas of Antarctica (Putzke and Pereira, 2001), although
moss communities are generally considered of low
complexity and species diversity (Smith, 1984).
In Antarctica, the mosses are associated to melting
areas, such that they depend of water supply during the
austral summer to realize photosynthesis and growing
(Schaefer et al., 2004; Meick and Seppelt, 1997). Given the
difficulties imposed by the environment, the mosses from
Antarctica present pigments that are involved in UV
radiation protection (Glime, 2007; Lovelock and Robinson,
2002), while some species are adapted to support
dehydration at different levels (Robinson et al., 2000).
The moss Antarctic flora can be divided into six
distinct phytogeographical elements (Ochyra, 1998)
comprising a number of species for each element, as
follows: Antarctic endemic distribution (11 species);
Subantarctic distribution (18 species); south-temperate
distribution (26 species); bipolar distribution; cosmopolitan
distribution (5 species); tropical distribution (1 species).
From this division, it can be observed that most of the
mosses found in Antarctica have bipolar distribution, being
a striking feature of the Antarctic moss flora (Ochyra et al.,
2008). However, the richness and other diversity stats
have not yet been widely exploited to understand the
distribution of moss species in Antarctic.
In this study, the distribution of moss species among
four different points from South Shetland and the
Antarctic continent was compared through a review of col-
lections, aiming to provide subsidies for the understanding
of how species are distributed in the Maritime Antarctic.

archipelago (King George - 62° 05′ 13, 55″S and 58° 24′
17, 51″W; Elephant - 61° 11′ 51, 74″S and 55° 17′ 56,
37″W; and Nelson Islands - 62° 14′ 29, 47″S and 58° 59′
39, 26″W) and one in the Antarctic Peninsula (Hope
Bay - 63° 23′ 0″S, 56° 59′ 0″W) were compared.
The collections were done in the ice-free areas during
the austral summers of years 1988, 1989, 1990, 1991,
1992, and 1994 in the King George, Elephant, and Nelson
Islands. In Hope Bay, the collections were made in
the 2009 summer (February). The distribution and occur-
rences reported by Ochyra et al. (2008) were also checked
for comparison purpose.
All collections were deposited in the HCB Herbarium
(Chaves Batista Herbarium). The species were indentified
according to Putzke and Pereira (2001), Ochyra (1998),
and Ochyra et al. (2008). The species names follow
Ochyra et al. (2008).
The data obtained about moss species growing in each
sampling area were organized in a presence or absence
(1 or 0, respectively) and quantitative matrices (number of
individual sampled) and used to describe the occurrence of
each species found. These matrices were used to obtain the

help of the PAST statistic program version 1.91 to evaluate

In the taxonomical review, 46 species were identified,

# THE GEOGRAPHICAL AFFINITIES OF THE MOSSES OF SOUTH AUSTRALIA 

# D. G. CATCHESIDE 1

> INTRODUCTION

South Australia has only 184 species of mosses, so far as is known. The follow-ing discussion of their distribution and geographical affinities is based on the data in 

my moss flora of the State (Catcheside 1980), together with additions and amendments gathered since it was compiled. The names used are those in that book, with minor exceptions. Many species are restricted in distribution to a few favourable habitats, especially in deep and moist gorges. To some extent, the small number in the State flora is due to imperfect exploration and therefore might be augmented by more through searches. Thus a few species (9 in all) are known in the southern mountains (Mac-Donnell Ranges) of the arid zone of the Northern Territory, but not yet in South Australia. Some of these may occur, particularly in the mountains of the North West of the State. Other species are found in both Victoria and Western Australia and a few of these could also be in the State. However, the total number is not likely finally to exceed 200 by very much, nor would any additions greatly affect the general conclusions that can now be drawn about the geographical affinities of the moss flora. The relative impoverishment of the moss flora is due to a number of factors of which aridity is a prominent one. About two thirds of the State enjoys less than 250 mm of rain per annum on the average and even this amount is very erratic in occurrence. Nevertheless the drier areas have a fairly rich moss flora, comprising species able to cope with aridity. Some 45 species are known to extend into areas with under 250 mm of rain per annum. These species are distinguished by the letter "A" in the appendix. If a less severe boundary between arid and semi-arid to humid a reas is adopted, as used by Arid Zone Research interests, some further 25 species, distinguished by the letter "a" in the appendix, are added to the list of arid zone mosses. It must be admitted that many are ephemerals and that others favour shel-tered habitats, often more permanently moist, as in gorges. Other factors restricting the richness of the flora are the predominantly basic substrates, which are often unstable as in the case of the sand dunes of the North East, the relative lack of acid humus, swamps and bogs and the lack of trees with stable bark. Thus there are only 12 aquatic species  ("Q"  in the appendix) and 11 corticolous ones ("R" in the appendix). The richest areas are the mountains a nd hills which are isolated from the richer, more humid Eastern Australia by dry plains. 1 Waite Agricult•Jral Research Institute, Glen Osmond, South Australia, 5064. 58 Journ . Hattori Bot. Lab. No. 52  I 9 8 2 However, even the wetter hills are subject to long periods of drought and heat in which mosses dry out. Hence the flora as a whole has a large proportion of ephem-eral species (at least 50) which evade the stress of drought by surviving as spores and of perennial species which are able to survive for long periods in a state of dryness. GEOGRAPHY OF SOUTH AUSTRALIAN MOSSES The known species are classified in Table sl and 2 (and in detail in the appendix according to their presence in other parts of the world (Wijk et al. 1959-1969, Magill & Schelpe 1979), particularly New Zealand (Austr 2), South America (Am 6), South Africa (Afr 4) and the Northern Hemisphere. Some do occur also in adjacent areas, but no record of this is made except for India (As 3), which is a large fragment of Gondwanaland. The mosses of South Australia scarcely have any affinity with the tropics. The grouping naturally suffers from the uncertainties about identity between mosses in different areas being given the same or different names. Increased know-ledge has separated some, for example Acrocladium chlamydophyllum in Australia and New Zealand is distinct from A . auricu/atum of South America (Andrews 1949, Karczmarz 1966), while what has been called Bartramia "stricta" in Australia is not the same as B. stricta in the Northern Hemisphere. There may be many of these homologous pairs of species, indicating divergent evolution . However, our know-ledge of mosses in the Southern Hemisphere lags behind that of the hepatics (e.g. Schuster 1979) in this respect.
